object_description: long four-storey volume defining an urban open space
design_condition: The long volume follows the avenue and defines an open space on the historic barracks axis, linking the two streets while leaving only a narrow perimeter path within the fenced site.

positive.statement: The elementary urban arrangement forms a worthy counterpart to the old barracks and plausibly defines the pedestrian connection between the two streets.
The open arched ground-floor structure makes the public purpose of the building tangible in a sophisticated way.
The office units can be flexibly organized around several courtyards.
The central upper-floor access allows clear orientation.
The courtyard typology gives the multispace and project-room modules a stringent organization.
The compact volumetrics achieve an efficient building envelope.
The consistent system separation has a lasting effect on component life-cycle costs.
The building concept allows plausible grading along the horizontal axis.
The themed courtyards create contrasting atmospheres and intelligently intertwine security and access functions.
Rainwater infiltration troughs create an interesting transition toward the avenue through relief, topography and varied vegetation.
The project conveys a surprising vision for a self-confident and open administrative center.
The proposal is based on clear urban-planning, typological and constructive logic.

negative.statement: The roof conflicts with the use of the space as bicycle parking and access to the underground car park.
The facade length along the avenue does not match the scale of the surrounding buildings.
The nearly fully occupied perimeter leaves only a narrow strip of outside space.
The architectural references appear somewhat additive and weaker than the basic concept.
The open arcade ground floor is contradicted by the occupation of non-public uses.
The upper-floor facade expression does not provide a congruent response to the interior or open-space ground.
The central access lacks connections to the courtyards, while closed corridors and artificially lit foyers can become confusing and labyrinthine.
The monumental hall landscape does not entirely correspond to the publicity of its use.
The above-average volume leads to higher costs than other contributions.
The tree structure makes only a timid statement relative to the imposing building size.
The design does not fully resolve the architecture congruently with its operational organization.
The thematic density creates contradictions among references, scale and use.
